detail.abstract: Trauma processing is often constrained by affective overload, avoidance, and fragmented memory, which can limit engagement with verbal therapies. Mechanisms enabling safe, graded access to traumatic material remain underexplored. This paper proposes embodied externalization as a candidate mechanism: creating stable, manipulable visual artifacts that allow individuals to engage with trauma without being overwhelmed. Coupled with co-witnessing by a therapist or peer, this approach provides relational containment, attention regulation, and iterative narrative integration. Drawing on empirical findings in art therapy, cognitive-somatic theory, and trauma neuroscience, we develop a conceptual model in which multisensory, motor-engaged creation enhances affect tolerance and supports memory reconsolidation. Tangible artifacts provide representational distance, enabling graded engagement that purely verbal or symbolic interventions may not achieve. The framework generates testable predictions regarding artifact-mediated affect regulation, co-witnessing effects, and longitudinal integration, illustrating how some art-based interventions implement the broader mechanism of embodied externalization. By clarifying these processes, this work moves research on art-based trauma interventions beyond descriptive claims, offering a falsifiable, mechanism-focused lens that bridges clinical observation and trauma neuroscience, and guiding future empirical investigations of interventions for trauma.

title: The Information Content of Second-party Opinions in the Sustainability-linked Bond Market
affiliations: SKEMA Business School, Bos Finance Solutions, SKEMA Business School - Lille Campus and

detail.title: The Information Content of Second-party Opinions in the Sustainability-linked Bond Market
detail.abstract: We analyze the information content of second-party opinion (SPO) ambition assessments in the sustainability-linked bond (SLB) market using a novel hand-collected dataset. Issuers of highly ambitious SLBs exhibit slightly larger subsequent reductions in emissions intensity, contain growth in absolute emissions more effectively, are more likely to miss sustainability targets, and earn higher announcement returns around the SPO disclosure date. In contrast, issuers of very low ambition SLBs experience negative returns and largely self-select out of the SLB market. These findings suggest SPO ambition assessments provide a credible signal of firms' commitments to sustainability. However, ambition does not predict reductions in absolute emissions, does not influence SLB pricing, and even among highly ambitious SLBs, announcement returns are largely insensitive to issuers' emissions levels and whether targets are science-based, pointing to a potential disconnect between the SLB market and societal decarbonization objectives.

detail.abstract: Business continuity and disaster recovery (BC/DR) are among the most pressing concerns for organizations operating critical infrastructure systems globally. As enterprises migrate workloads to hybrid cloud environments spanning on-premises data centers, Microsoft Azure, and Amazon Web Services (AWS), the complexity of maintaining recoverability increases substantially. This paper presents a practical, battle-tested framework for designing and implementing automated disaster recovery strategies in hybrid cloud environments, drawn from over 12 years of experience managing production systems in the telecommunications sector. The framework addresses Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) through automated failover mechanisms, cross-region replication, infrastructure-as-code provisioning, and continuous DR testing. Implementation of this framework across enterprise telecommunications systems reduced RTO from 8 hours to under 30 minutes and RPO from 24 hours to under 5 minutes, while reducing annual DR operational costs by 45%.

title: The Algorithmic General Partner: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Philosophy, and the Moral Architecture of Venture Capital and Private Equity

detail.title: The Algorithmic General Partner: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Philosophy, and the Moral Architecture of Venture Capital and Private Equity

detail.abstract: This paper examines the accelerating integration of Artificial Intelligence into private capital markets, specifically Venture Capital (VC) and Private Equity (PE), through a tripartite lens of epistemic philosophy, financial theory, and moral reasoning. As AI systems assume roles once exclusively held by human general partners, fundamental questions arise about the nature of judgment, the architecture of institutional responsibility, and the moral legitimacy of algorithmic capital allocation. Drawing on philosophical traditions from Aristotelian phronesis to Kantian deontology and contemporary epistemic virtue theory, this paper argues that AI's adoption in private markets is not merely a technological transition but an ontological disruption, one that restructures how knowledge is produced, how risk is evaluated, and how moral accountability is distributed. The paper proposes a Moral Architecture Framework (MAF) for AI-augmented investment institutions and examines empirical patterns in AI-driven deal sourcing, due diligence, valuation, and portfolio management. It further interrogates the epistemic risks inherent in pattern-based intelligence deployed in fundamentally uncertain, narrative-driven markets. Ultimately, this work contends that the most consequential question for AI in private markets is not whether machines can outperform humans, but whether the values embedded in their architectures are those we consciously choose to institutionalize.

title: HLER: Human-in-the-Loop Economic Research via Multi-agent Pipelines for Empirical Discovery

detail.title: HLER: Human-in-the-Loop Economic Research via Multi-agent Pipelines for Empirical Discovery

declarations.funderStatement: Chen Zhu was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72573164), the Pinduoduo-China Agricultural University Research Fund (Grant No. PC2024B02011), and the 2115 Talent Development Program at China Agricultural University.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent-based systems that attempt to automate scientific research workflows. Existing approaches often pursue fully autonomous discovery, in which AI systems generate research ideas, conduct experiments, and produce manuscripts with minimal human involvement. However, empirical research in economics and the social sciences poses additional challenges: research questions must be grounded in available datasets, identification strategies require careful design, and human judgment remains essential for evaluating economic significance. We introduce HLER (Human-in-the-Loop Economic Research), a multi-agent architecture that supports empirical research automation while preserving critical human oversight. The system orchestrates specialized agents for data auditing, data profiling, hypothesis generation, econometric analysis, manuscript drafting, and automated review. A central design principle is dataset-aware hypothesis generation, in which candidate research questions are constrained by dataset structure, variable availability, and distributional diagnostics. This prevents infeasible or hallucinated hypotheses that frequently arise in unconstrained LLM ideation. HLER further introduces a two-loop research architecture: a question quality loop in which candidate hypotheses are generated, screened for feasibility, and selected by a human researcher; and a research revision loop in which automated review triggers re-analysis and manuscript revision. Human decision gates are embedded at key stages, including question selection and publication approval, allowing researchers to steer the automated pipeline. We evaluate the framework on three empirical datasets, including longitudinal survey data. Across 14 pipeline runs, dataset-aware hypothesis generation produces feasible research questions in 87% of cases, compared with 41% under unconstrained generation, and the system successfully completes end-to-end empirical manuscripts at an average API cost of $0.8-$1.5 per run. A detailed case study on the China Health and Nutrition Survey illustrates the full workflow from data inspection to a revised draft manuscript. These results suggest that Human-AI collaborative pipelines may provide a practical path toward scalable empirical research. The HLER working paper repository is publicly available at https://github.com/maxwell2732/hler-working-papers.

title: Work Authorization Delays and Economic Integration of Asylum Seekers in the United States
affiliations: University of Texas at El Paso - Department of Economics and Finance and San Diego State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Work Authorization Delays and Economic Integration of Asylum Seekers in the United States
detail.abstract: Access to the labor market is crucial for the economic integration of asylum seekers. This study estimates the causal impact of work authorization timing on the labor market outcomes of likely asylum seekers. We link USCIS administrative records with American Community Survey microdata and use congestion-driven variation in processing times within an instrumental variable framework. Faster authorization boosts labor force participation, employment, and earnings, while effects on hours worked and occupational choices are modest. The impacts are concentrated within the first decade after arrival and diminish over time, indicating that processing delays slow integration but do not permanently hinder it.

detail.title: U.S. Trade Policy and Partner Industrial Production
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamic transmission of bilateral United States tariff shocks to the industrial production in 83 of its trading partners across varying time horizons. Utilizing a comprehensive monthly panel dataset spanning from January 1989 to October 2025, the study implements a panel local projection strategy alongside a bias-correcting split-panel jackknife estimator to mitigate incidental parameter bias and capture complex, non-linear trade policy effects. The empirical results reveal that aggregate industrial production drops by 1.7% by the thirty-month horizon following a unit (1%) shock of U.S. tariffs. A detailed sectoral decomposition uncovers significant sectoral divergence: capital formation in the construction sector of free-trade-agreement partners collapses significantly, whereas their manufacturing sector demonstrates substantial stickiness and long-term expansion. Furthermore, the analysis identifies a volatile boom-bust cycle of spatial trade diversion in long-distance trading partners and severe upstream mining contractions in financially constrained economies lacking access to external credit. Considering differences between development levels yields highly different trajectories: advanced economies experience delayed aggregate contractions despite short-term manufacturing resilience, whereas emerging markets suffer immediate upstream damage. These findings challenge homogeneous macroeconomic policy responses, suggesting that policymakers must deploy precise, regime-dependent strategies to protect domestic capital formation and manage the structural vulnerabilities exposed by prolonged trade uncertainty.

title: The Emergence of Regional Cultures in the United States
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder and Chapman University - The George L. Argyros College of Business and Economics

detail.title: The Emergence of Regional Cultures in the United States
detail.abstract: This paper recovers the cultural geography of the United States from first-name patterns in census data spanning 1850 to 1930. Using unsupervised clustering of county-level name distributions, we identify spatially coherent cultural regions that align with historically recognized settlement patterns and remain stable across eight decades of economic and institutional change. The deepest division separates North from South, but finer groupings (New England, the Mid-Atlantic, Appalachia, the Deep South) emerge as nested subregions. Formal tests confirm that the recovered clusters are spatially contiguous, temporally persistent, and robust to resampling. The findings bear on whether liberal institutions require cultural homogeneity, whether cultural pluralism is a source of resilience or fragility, and how the imprint of early settlement shapes the practice of self-governance.

detail.title: The Development of Corporate Governance in Australia

publicationDetails.detailsText: Christine Mallin (editor), Handbook on International Corporate Governance, Country Analyses, 2nd edition, 2012, Edward Elgar

detail.abstract: This chapter reviews corporate governance in Australia. The approach adopted is to look at several corporate governance mechanisms; that is, mechanisms that play a role in decreasing the divergence between managers’ and shareholders’ interests that Jensen and Meckling articulated in their famous 1976 article. The mechanisms reviewed are: market forces (particularly the market for corporate control and product market competition); the legal environment protecting investors; monitoring by shareholders (particularly large blockholders and institutional investors) and proxy advisers; monitoring by non-executive directors; disclosure rules and governance codes; independent audit; and incentive compensation for senior executives. The chapter illustrates that while many aspects of the corporate governance regime in Australia are similar to those in countries like the US and the UK, there are some features of the Australian regime that distinguish it, for example, the incidence and role of large blockholders. But, fundamentally, Australia has a relatively well-developed capital market, and its governance environment is generally reflective of shareholder primacy.

detail.abstract: This paper challenges the conventional divide between productive and non-productive assets by proposing that scarcity is the fundamental economic origin of value across all asset classes, with internal cash flow generation serving as a primary structural mechanism for its realization. We develop a valuation framework in which scarcity is modeled as a latent, time-varying state variable shaped by economic pressures on demand and supply, estimable via state-space methods. A class of monetization functions maps these scarcity states into observable or forecasted cash flows, allowing discounted cash flow (DCF) logic to be reinterpreted as a universal pricing mechanism for intertemporal scarcity. The framework accommodates both terminal-value assets, such as Bitcoin or gold, and income-generating assets, such as equities or bonds. While we establish an algebraic duality between terminal and periodic payoff structures, we highlight the real-world economic frictions, such as reinvestment risk and liquidity constraints, that separate them in practice. Finally, we classify assets according to their foundational scarcity mechanisms, whether physical, contractual, algorithmic, or reputational.

title: Diminishing Transparency: A Critical Analysis of India's Right to Information Act and Lessons from Nepal
affiliations: Christ (Deemed to be University), Pune, Lavasa

detail.title: Diminishing Transparency: A Critical Analysis of India's Right to Information Act and Lessons from Nepal
detail.abstract:
Although it is a notable legislative intervention of India’s transparency architecture, the Right to Information Act of 2005 demonstrates a clear disconnect between effectiveness in operation and statutory sophistication. This paper synthesizes and assesses academic scholarship that includes doctoral jurisprudence, empirical studies, comparative institutional analysis, and critical policy values in order to examine the constitutional history, implementation strategies, and systematic barriers of RTI over its two decades of existence. The research reveals a crucial impasse: India’s RTI loss rank sixth globally for statutory quality, yet their effectiveness and implementation rank sixty-sixth, indicating several enforcement flaws that seriously undermine the law’s capacity to achieve transformative social changes. The evolution of informational rights under legal framework demonstrated how judicial activism translated implicit rights under Article 19(1)(a)[1] into explicit statutory architecture, redefining transparency as a normative standard of democracy rather than a legislative peculiarity.

The effectiveness of RTI is perpetually undermined by seven significant operational pathologies; the 2019 amendment’s[2] erosion of Information Commission’s independence through executive control over tenure and compensation; the strategic deployment of exemption provisions as obfuscation  mechanisms; the continued exemption of publicly-funded political parties from disclosure requirements despite explicit judicial directives; the ineffectiveness of penalty provisions as deterrents; widespread bureaucratic resistance manifested through personal vacancies, procedural delays and antiquated record management processes, complete non-compliance with proactive disclosure mandates under Section 4[3]; and the absence of adequate whistleblower protections framework highlighted by documented activist deaths. Comparative analysis with Nepal’s RTI framework reveals instructive lessons regarding institutional device design, enforcement mechanisms and civil society mobilization. Important gaps remain in present research including comparative institutional studies and evaluating progressive transparency models; intersectional analyses investigating disparate access patterns among marginal communities; technological integration evaluations assessing digital governance applications; and longitudinal econometric analyses linking RTI utilization with corruption indices. Realizing the RTI’s democratic potential necessitates prioritizing sectoral efficiency evaluations, technology-enabled transparency innovations, rigorous impact assessments, and comprehensive enforcement architecture reconstitution beyond merely symbolic legislative compliance.

title: Terminal Sinks: Monetary Circulation Failure as the Primary Economic Risk of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Terminal Sinks: Monetary Circulation Failure as the Primary Economic Risk of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: Economic analysis of artificial intelligence has converged on a displacement narrative: jobs lost, wages suppressed, inequality widened. This paper argues that framing targets the symptom while missing the underlying pathology. We introduce the concept of the terminal sink, defined as an economic actor that captures market value without returning it to the monetary circulation system through wages, local consumption, or supply chain spend. We argue that AI inference systems function as terminal sinks at scale, and that their proliferation constitutes a circulation failure, a structural disruption to the velocity and density of money flow through the middle economy that is both distinct from and more damaging than labor displacement alone. Using an extended Leontief input-output framework, we show that AI's near-zero backward linkages cause the economy-wide spending multiplier to contract as AI substitution rises, even under GDP-stable assumptions. We further introduce the Circulation Density Index (CDI), a graph-theoretic metric defined over the transaction network of an economy, which captures the throughput behavior of individual economic actors and aggregates to a system-level diagnostic. We demonstrate formally that CDI declines as high-throughput nodes, namely wage-earning workers and local businesses, are replaced by low-throughput nodes such as AI systems, and that this decline is invisible to standard macroeconomic indicators including GDP, employment rate, and the Gini coefficient. The paper concludes that the policy debate over AI's economic impact is asking the wrong question: the risk is not unemployment in aggregate but the progressive desiccation of transactional density in the middle economy, and addressing it requires new diagnostic tools before it can require new policy.

title: Transfer Across Operating Conditions for Fault Severity Estimation in Gears
affiliations: , Ben-Gurion University of the Negev - Department of Mechanical Engineering, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev - Department of Mechanical Engineering and Ben Gurion University

detail.title: Transfer Across Operating Conditions for Fault Severity Estimation in Gears
detail.abstract: Accurately estimating the severity of faults in gears is crucial for effective prognostics and condition based maintenance. Fault severity estimation is a key element in system reliability management and setting up of digital twins. This study proposes a new algorithm for estimating the severity of faults in gears, drawing on concepts of conceptual thinking. The algorithm transfers knowledge on a system across different operating conditions and generalizes fault severity estimates from simulation to reality by learning boundaries of meaning for an operational profile which is based on other profiles. The algorithm has been successfully tested in two use cases, where it learned one operating condition and applied to a new one. The combination of fault severity definitions with boundary of meaning and a transfer learning algorithm provides a general engineering motivated effective approach to fault severity prediction.

title: The Hidden Variable in the Growth Function: Demon

detail.title: The Hidden Variable in the Growth Function: Demon

keywords: Economic Growth Moral–Spiritual Dynamics Cobb–Douglas Production Function Moral Degradation Index (D) Ethical Cost of Economic Activity Technological Progress Capital Accumulation GDP Growth Long-Term Economic Stability Historical Economic Patterns Domination and Exploitation Innovation and Development Moral Efficiency Frontier Production vs. Conscience Balance

detail.abstract: This paper advances a theoretical model linking economic growth to moral-spiritual dynamics. By extending the classical Cobb–Douglas production function, we introduce a fifth factor — the Demon or  Moral Degradation Index (D) — representing the ethical cost associated with economic activity. The model posits that while technological progress and capital accumulation expand GDP in the short run, they also intensify D, thereby undermining long-term stability. Using historical patterns from medieval Europe to the digital era, the study demonstrates that domination and exploitation, rather than pure innovation, were principal accelerators of economic ascent. The resulting framework—termed the Moral Efficiency Frontier—proposes a calculus of balance between production and conscience.

title: Measuring Elite Capture of the Education Earnings Premium: The Carnoy Index
affiliations: Stanford University - Graduate School of Education, Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Economics, Queen Mary University of London and São Paulo University

detail.title: Measuring Elite Capture of the Education Earnings Premium: The Carnoy Index

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding to disclose.

detail.abstract: One of the leading reasons behind social inequities is that elite groups have had access to more widespread and higher-quality educational opportunities much earlier, often when their economic returns were much higher. Nonetheless, measures of educational inequities tend to focus exclusively on contemporary differences, and often, only within the school-age population. This paper proposes a new measure -- the Carnoy index -- that captures historical and contemporary differences in the access to the economic returns of education across different groups. Concretely, the Carnoy index is the share of the cumulative education earnings premium accrued by the elite over time in excess to that accrued by other groups. The paper advances a methodology to compute the index using household survey data, and illustrates its applications by computing it along wealth, race and gender dimensions, within primary, secondary and post-secondary education, for twelve countries and territories with compatible data (1980-2011; N = 261 million). We showcase the new insights that the Carnoy index brings relative to other measures when it comes to understanding educational inequities and informing policies to address them.

title: The Role of Digital Identity Frameworks in Catalyzing African Financial and Regulatory Integration

detail.title: The Role of Digital Identity Frameworks in Catalyzing African Financial and Regulatory Integration
detail.abstract: As digitalization transforms the landscape of global governance and commerce, "Digital Identity" has shifted from a mere technical credential to a foundational pillar of socioeconomic development. This paper investigates the strategic implementation of digital identity frameworks within the African context, examining the interplay between foundational, functional, and transactional models as catalysts for regional integration. By analyzing the specific trajectories of African nations-such as Nigeria's biometric integration and Rwanda's decentralized service portals-alongside international benchmarks like India's Aadhaar and Estonia's e-Residency, this research explores how digital identifiers address the "identity gap" emphasized by UN SDG 16.9. The study further evaluates the tension between centralized state-led registries and decentralized architectures in the pursuit of financial inclusion and democratic integrity. Finally, the paper addresses the unique implementation hurdles faced by African states-including infrastructure limitations, interoperability, and cybersecurity-while advocating for legal frameworks and data minimization strategies that align with both global standards (like GDPR) and local digital sovereignty imperatives.

title: State Violence and the Terrorism Label: Gaza, Iran, and the Legal Boundary between War and Terrorism

detail.title: State Violence and the Terrorism Label: Gaza, Iran, and the Legal Boundary between War and Terrorism
detail.abstract: This paper examines how international law distinguishes between terrorism and warfare and asks whether similar forms of violence are categorized differently depending on whether the actor involved is a state or a non-state organization. Terrorism is widely described in international discourse as violence directed against civilians for the purpose of intimidation or political coercion. In practice, however, the terrorism label is applied primarily to non-state actors, while state violence is evaluated through the legal frameworks governing armed conflict and selfdefense. Using doctrinal legal analysis and comparative case studies, the paper examines two contemporary contexts: Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and military confrontations involving Iran, Israel, and the United States. The analysis evaluates these conflicts using widely cited elements of terrorism—violence affecting civilian populations, the generation of fear or intimidation, and the use of violence to influence political behavior—and compares these elements with the legal frameworks governing warfare. The study argues that international law applies the concept of terrorism asymmetrically. Violence committed by non-state actors is commonly classified as terrorism, while comparable forms of coercive violence undertaken by states are interpreted as warfare or potential violations of international humanitarian law. This distinction reflects the institutional structure of international law, which regulates state conduct through the law of armed conflict rather than terrorism law. By examining conflicts involving Gaza and Iran within a unified analytical framework, the paper demonstrates that the boundary between terrorism and warfare is shaped not only by the nature of violent acts but also by the identity of the actors who carry them out.

detail.abstract: Donors' quests for more sophisticated, strategic and connected ways of philanthropic giving, long prominent in the United States, are now ubiquitous around the world. This is one factor in the stratospheric expansion of 'donor-advised funds' (DAFs), a form of philanthropic vehicle that enables donors to give to a public charity-including community foundations-claiming an immediate tax deduction, while retaining rights to advise the charity on how to distribute those funds later. The popularity of DAFs has expanded to the Asia Pacific, where many jurisdictions now provide public philanthropic intermediaries as an institutional response to donor desires. DAFs have been controversial in the United States, while analysis in other jurisdictions has been limited. This article identifies key concerns raised in the US context and compares the institutional responses of Singapore, Japan and Australia, focussing on the degree to which the responses address those concerns, whilst still retaining the advantages of intermediaries. In doing so it identifies that different regulatory approaches are possible, and likely desirable, due to differences between the three jurisdictions. The analysis also helps to predict whether public philanthropic intermediaries are likely to become a significant feature of the philanthropic landscape in Singapore, Japan and Australia.

title: The Illusion of Safety: Quantifying the Impact of Macroeconomic Friction and Sequence of Tax Risk in Monte Carlo Simulations

detail.title: The Illusion of Safety: Quantifying the Impact of Macroeconomic Friction and Sequence of Tax Risk in Monte Carlo Simulations

detail.abstract:
Industry-Standard Monte Carlo (ISMC) software typically evaluates retirement readiness within a static-macroeconomic vacuum—projecting current-law tax brackets and linear inflation over multi-decade horizons. This structural blind spot systematically overestimates portfolio survivability. This research introduces the SLATE (Stochastic Longitudinal Assessment of Tax Exposure) framework, a stochastic Monte Carlo engine designed to subject simulated lifetimes to compounding historical frictions: actuarial mortality, inflation volatility, sequence of returns risk, and Markov-driven historical tax regime volatility.

When subjected to empirical macroeconomic friction (calibrated to 50 years of U.S. data), median terminal wealth for mass-affluent savers compresses by over 90% relative to standard ISMC projections. This stark pre-retirement wealth suppression aligns seamlessly with empirical Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) data. Furthermore, during decumulation, heavy reliance on tax-deferred (Traditional) vehicles acts as a latent systemic liability. When a highly compounded late-life morbidity shock forces outsized capital liquidations during periods of historical bracket compression, retirees must disproportionately gross-up withdrawals. This Sequence of Tax Risk severely fractures portfolio survivability at elevated withdrawal rates. The data mathematically demonstrates that tax-exempt (All-Roth) decumulation neutralizes this risk, serving not merely as a tax-efficiency tool, but as a foundational structural defense against macroeconomic volatility.

title: Women in the Legal Profession in Malawi: Past, Present and the Future

detail.title: Women in the Legal Profession in Malawi: Past, Present and the Future
detail.abstract: This article explores the evolving profile of women in the legal profession in Malawi from the past to the present and forecasts for the future. The study examines historical gender equality using case law and the stories of Malawian women pioneers in the legal profession. The study presents empirical findings to show the state of gender equality in the legal profession in Malawi. The findings show that there has been an improvement in the entry of women into the legal profession and a reduction of obvious forms of bias. Women have not only entered the profession but have also occupied various leadership positions in various sectors. However, there are low numbers of women-led law firms in Malawi. The research found that subtle barriers in the form of a lack of support, mentorship, and networking are possible contributing factors to the low number of women leaders in law firms. The article suggests that the legal profession can promote inclusivity, fairness, and equal opportunities, particularly in law firms, by addressing the subtle forms of bias.

detail.abstract: To find the factors influencing banking system liquidity, this study analyzes the liquidity behavior in the banking system of Bangladesh and finally examines its influences using an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model with cointegration techniques and error correction term. The study finds that the growth of liquidity in the banking system is positively associated with the change of foreign credit and negatively influenced by the return rate difference between real saving certificates rate and real bank deposit rate, overnight money market rate (call money rate) and some liquidity and stock market linked policy turning points, categorized as dummy variable in the paper. The model establishes a long run relation between banking system liquidity and its tested variables. However, if the variables influence liquidity in different way the new interrelation may sustain for 6 months at best and after that the original relationship will return.

title: Beyond the Sale: How Shopping Festivals Shape Consumer Behavior and Retail Outcomes Online
affiliations: and The Chinese University of Hong Kong - CUHK Business School

detail.title: Beyond the Sale: How Shopping Festivals Shape Consumer Behavior and Retail Outcomes Online
detail.abstract: Large-scale shopping festivals have become a central promotional format in online retail, yet their effects extend beyond short-term sales growth. Using two years of transaction-level data from a leading e-commerce platform in China, covering more than 577 million orders from approximately 60 million consumers in 331 cities and 4,369 active retailers distributed across 147 cities, we examine how shopping festivals shape consumer behavior and retail outcomes along multiple dimensions. We find that festivals generate substantial demand expansion, but also change how consumers time and evaluate purchases, leading to greater temporal concentration, increased work-hour shopping, and higher return rates. These effects are largely confined to festival windows, with little evidence of intertemporal substitution outside the event periods. Moreover, responses are highly heterogeneous across products and retailers: sales gains are concentrated in specific categories, whereas elevated return rates and their associated costs disproportionately affect small and medium-sized sellers, revealing a fundamental trade-off in event-driven promotions.

title: PISRA: A Parsimonious Prudential Early-Warning Indicator of Bank Failure

detail.title: PISRA: A Parsimonious Prudential Early-Warning Indicator of Bank Failure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper develops and validates PISRA, a parsimonious prudential early-warning indicator of bank failure grounded in the view that bank distress is not a random rupture but the cumulative outcome of structural fragility building across core balance-sheet dimensions. Using a large quarterly panel of U.S. commercial banks over 2001-2025 linked to subsequent failure events, the paper evaluates predictive performance at 4-quarter, 8-quarter, and 12-quarter horizons under a strict out-ofsample design with temporal separation, train-only preprocessing, and sigmoid probability calibration. The results show strong and unusually stable performance across all three horizons, with Test AUC remaining close to 0.94 throughout, while preserving sound probabilistic calibration in an extreme rare-event setting with failure rates below 0.2%. The evidence further indicates that PISRA remains economically interpretable and operationally usable under supervisory alert thresholds, perturbation exercises, capital-dose experiments, and historical stress recognition. Benchmark comparisons show that richer nonlinear alternatives do not overturn the central result that a compact supervisory accounting architecture remains highly competitive. Robustness checks, including distributional stability analysis, bootstrap resampling, and placebo leakage auditing, further support the conclusion that the model's performance reflects genuine predictive signal rather than incidental fit or temporal contamination. Taken together, the findings position PISRA as a transparent, scalable, and institutionally credible framework for prudential monitoring, supervisory stress testing, capital planning, and broader systemic-risk assessment.

title: Australian Social Services Scandals: Towards Dystopia? Or Equity and Justice for the Vulnerable?
affiliations: The University of Sydney Law School

detail.title: Australian Social Services Scandals: Towards Dystopia? Or Equity and Justice for the Vulnerable?
detail.abstract: This Lecture explores the harm and injustices experienced by vulnerable Australians due to social services program failures such as robodebt, employment services income support sanctioning, and the apportionment scandals. I also deal with concerns about proposed changes to the way National Disability Insurance Scheme ('NDIS') budgets are determined. I argue that while legal protections and remedies have been well renovated to accommodate individual social security grievances (restoring fidelity to liberal values), law reform has failed adequately to address either the systemic harms and mass grievances (a failure to guarantee socioeconomic values such as distributional justice), or to develop preventive counters to structural forces that give rise to such failures. I suggest that avenues of redress for social services (such as the NDIS) provide even less by way of individual or systemic justice. I conclude that the mainly extra-legal successes of other governance measures may offer a better response to systemic injustices in social services.

title: The 'Sleeping Giant': A Behavioral Anomaly in Prediction Markets

detail.title: The 'Sleeping Giant': A Behavioral Anomaly in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: This paper explores a behavioral phenomenon in sports economics: human tendencies to overbet on more well-known teams-known as "dynasties"-in playoff series, especially when these teams are statistical underdogs. In an emerging world of prediction markets, it is important to not only identify market inefficiencies but also to understand the underlying behavioral factors, as this phenomenon may be present in other liquid markets. Using 12 seasons of NBA betting data (2008-2020) with Elo-based benchmarks, this study found betting markets tend to overprice dynasty underdogs by a mean bias of +10.43 percentage points (p < 0.0001), while non-dynasty underdogs show no statistically significant bias (+0.08pp, p = 0.82), confirming the effect is identity-specific rather than general model error. This mispricing yields a betting strategy with +15.81% gross ROI (62.9% win rate) and persists across the full 12-season sample despite high market liquidity. These findings show that bettors systematically overweight team reputation, creating mispricings that persist despite being exploitable.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the presence of foreign women employed in domestic and care services enables adult Italian women to delay retirement decisions and remain in the labor force. To this end, the analysis exploits the sharp and unexpected increase in Romanian immigration into the domestic and personal care sector in Italy following the 2007 EU enlargement. Focusing on the period 2007-2011, prior to the implementation of the 2012 Monti-Fornero pension reform, the study uses linked administrative and survey data on the working trajectories of Italian women aged 55 and over, together with a shift-share instrumental variable strategy, to estimate the causal effect of local exposure to Romanian women on retirement, employment, and unemployment probabilities. The results show that a higher local presence of Romanian women, potentially employed in the domestic and personal care sector, significantly reduces the probability of retirement and increases employment, with no effect on unemployment. The effects are stronger for unmarried women, for those with higher levels of education and income, and in areas characterized by limited availability of residential elderly care facilities. No comparable effects are found for men, supporting the interpretation of a substitution mechanism in household production.

title: Distributional-Aggregate Feedback in the Macroeconomic Effects of National Minimum Wage Shocks

detail.title: Distributional-Aggregate Feedback in the Macroeconomic Effects of National Minimum Wage Shocks
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the distributional and macroeconomic effects of minimum wage shocks in Korea using a functional vector autoregression (fVAR) model. I find that a positive minimum wage shock reduces household income and the employment rates of household heads, with the most pronounced declines at the bottom of the distribution. Because the income contraction driven by severe job losses is disproportionately concentrated among vulnerable households, relative inequality worsens, leading to a significant increase in the Gini index. Departing from the existing fVAR literature, I demonstrate that incorporating cross-sectional information is quantitatively crucial for estimating aggregate effects. Specifically, the negative aggregate employment response is primarily driven by the endogenous responses of low-income households; ignoring these distributional feedbacks within a standard VAR framework renders the aggregate employment decline statistically insignificant and masks the true inflationary pressures. These findings suggest that the minimum wage may be an inefficient policy tool for correcting labor market frictions.

title: Decision Alignment Theory: Structural Misalignment and Organisational Decision Latency

detail.title: Decision Alignment Theory: Structural Misalignment and Organisational Decision Latency
detail.abstract: Traditional organisational theory often ascribes quality failure and decision latency to individual management competency or hierarchical depth (D). This paper proposes Decision Alignment Theory (DAT), a structural framework suggesting that organisational performance is predominantly constrained not by the number of layers in the hierarchy, but by the alignment, or misalignment, between Decision Authority (A) and Decision Consequence (C). This paper introduces the Structural Misalignment Set (Sa) - This is a formal metric for identifying the density of authority-consequence gaps, as the primary driver of systemic friction. When Authority (A) and Consequence (C) diverge, two predictable pathologies come into view: • Authority Gravity: This is where Consequence (C) exceeds Authority (A) (C>A), triggers terminal node saturation through upward decision migration. • Accountability Abdication: This is where Authority (A) exceeds Consequence (C) (A>C) degrades decision quality through moral hazard. This Theory demonstrates that decision latency emerges from the interaction between the initial hierarchal distance and the structural friction created when Consequence and Authority separate along the decision path. The Model demonstrates that multiple organisations that hold identical hierarchal depth (D) can display differing performance based on their density of structural asymmetry. DAT can provide a diagnostic tool for identifying latent latency and structural fragility by isolating misalignment as a discrete physical property of the organisation.

title: Structural Change and Resource Productivity in European Economies: Implications for Global Sustainability Governance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Structural Change and Resource Productivity in European Economies: Implications for Global Sustainability Governance
detail.abstract: The continued growth of global material use poses a major challenge to achieving sustainability goals. Increasing resource productivity is frequently promoted as a pathway to decoupling economic growth from material consumption, yet evidence of absolute decoupling remains limited. Recent global assessments highlight that such outcomes depend not only on efficiency gains, but on deeper structural transformations of economic systems.This paper investigates how structural change shapes resource productivity trajectories in European economies and examines the implications of these dynamics for global sustainability governance. Using a comparative analysis of 31 European countries between 2000 and 2015, countries are grouped according to shared trends in resource productivity growth. An integrated framework combining economy-wide material flow analysis with monetary and physical input-output tables is then applied to characterize sectoral dynamics within each group.The results revealed distinct structural pathways with different resource productivity outcomes. Economies with limited progress remain reliant on material-intensive sectors, while higher productivity growth is associated with structural shifts towards less intensive activities accompanied by broad declines in domestic material use across sectors.While acknowledging that service-oriented economies may externalize part of their material demand through imports, the findings demonstrate that structural change is a necessary precondition for decoupling, though not sufficient in isolation. The paper provides sectoral evidence on how different economic structures influence resource productivity, highlighting the importance of aligning domestic structural transformation with trade and consumption-based governance mechanisms. The results offer insights relevant to the design of policies aimed at reducing material use while maintaining economic performance.

title: The Anxiety of Embedded Officials: Local Ties and Bureaucratic Compliance during China's Anti-Gang Crackdown (2018-20)

detail.title: The Anxiety of Embedded Officials: Local Ties and Bureaucratic Compliance during China's Anti-Gang Crackdown (2018-20)
detail.abstract: Conventional wisdom in Chinese politics suggests that officials with local ties are more vulnerable to the influence of social elites and less compliant with central policies. This paper questions this view and proposes a more nuanced relationship between local embeddedness and bureaucratic compliance in China. It argues that, when a centrally mandated policy has high political priority and could adversely affect certain local interests, bureaucrats with stronger local ties may face greater suspicion of obstructing its implementation. To avoid scrutiny and protect themselves from punishment, they are incentivized to enforce such policies more intensely. This paper tests the theory using city-level data from China’s National Crackdown on Gang Crimes (2018–2020), a campaign targeting organized criminal groups and their obscure connections to local officials. The findings show that prefecture-level city leaders with stronger ties to their assigned localities made more aggressive efforts to prosecute organized crime members. This study offers unique insights into how local embeddedness shapes bureaucratic behavior: the fear of being perceived as complicit may drive localized officials to “overcompensate” in implementing central mandates.

title: Trust as a Dierential Filter: Mathematical Foundations for Cross-Cultural Analysis of Prepaid Consumption

detail.title: Trust as a Dierential Filter: Mathematical Foundations for Cross-Cultural Analysis of Prepaid Consumption
detail.abstract: Prepaid consumption patterns vary strikingly across institutional environments: consumers in high-trust markets readily deposit money into merchant accounts, while consumers in low-trust markets reject stored-value deposits yet accept service vouchers of identical monetary value. This paper provides the mathematical foundations for analyzing such cross-cultural divergence. We model a bilateral service market with heterogeneous consumers and endogenous merchant strategy adjustment, dening a contract typology ordered by risk encodingthe degree to which prepaid stakes retain moneylike versus goods-like psychological character. Three results form the theoretical core. The Mechanism Separation Theorem proves that, under equalexpenditure conditions, any population-level gap between voucher and storedvalue acceptance must originate from the trust channel rather than liquidity constraints. The Trust Collapse Theorem establishes sucient conditions for market-wide trust failure when default contagion outpaces adaptive learning. The Equilibrium Trichotomy maps institutional trust levels to three qualitatively distinct market regimesstored-value dominance, property-type substitution, and prepaid extinctionproviding structural predictions testable across societies.

title: Autoregressive Distributed Lag with Seemingly Unrelated Regression (SUR) Framework for Panel Cointegration Test

detail.title: Autoregressive Distributed Lag with Seemingly Unrelated Regression (SUR) Framework for Panel Cointegration Test
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a system-based extension of the autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach by embedding it within the Seemingly Unrelated Regression (SUR) framework of Zellner (1962). The proposed SUR-ARDL methodology allows for heterogeneous short-run dynamics and country-specific long-run relationships while explicitly accounting for contemporaneous cross-sectional dependence. By jointly estimating country-specific error-correction models, the approach improves efficiency and robustness of cointegration inference relative to conventional single-equation ARDL procedures. An empirical application to the renewable energy consumption-economic growth nexus in selected ASEAN economies illustrates the practical relevance of the proposed framework.

title: Do Gasoline Price Changes Shift Mobility Choices? Evidence from German Walking Behavior

detail.title: Do Gasoline Price Changes Shift Mobility Choices? Evidence from German Walking Behavior
detail.abstract: Gasoline price policies are central to transportation decarbonization, yet little is known about whether higher fuel costs shift behavior toward non-motorized travel. This paper examines how gasoline price changes affect walking in Germany using regional daily step data from consumer wearables between 2020 and 2022. I study walking responses to both routine gasoline price fluctuations and large, salient price shocks. I find robust evidence that higher gasoline prices causally increase walking. Responses are modest for routine price variation but substantially larger for policy-driven shocks. By contrast, I find no clear evidence that geopolitical-conflict-driven price shocks generate a larger response than routine fluctuations. Overall, the findings suggest that fuel price policies can induce low-carbon mobility shifts along an overlooked margin and may also generate meaningful short-run health co-benefits through increased walking.

title: Financial uncertainty, climate risks, and climate-exposed assets: Evidence from time-varying and quantile-based analysis
affiliations: Notre Dame University, Hankuk University of Foreign Studies,  and Department of Economics, Pusan National University

detail.title: Financial uncertainty, climate risks, and climate-exposed assets: Evidence from time-varying and quantile-based analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines how financial uncertainty and climate risks transmit to climate-exposed investment assets, with particular attention to time-varying dependence, distributional asymmetry, and regime-specific predictability. Using weekly data on ESG equities (ESGU, SUSA), clean energy stocks (ICLN), carbon allowance assets (KRBN), and blockchain technology investments (BLOK), we employ an integrated empirical framework combining a Dynamic Conditional Correlation (DCC)-GARCH model, quantile-on-quantile (QQ) regression, and quantile-on-quantile Granger causality (QQGC). The results show that these assets are not insulated from systemic uncertainty, as their correlations with financial volatility are time-varying and often highly persistent, implying that diversification benefits can weaken in turbulent market conditions when they are most needed. Quantile-based evidence reveals pronounced asymmetry and asset-specific heterogeneity: for broad ESG equities, effects are relatively uniform across return quantiles, while for clean energy and blockchain assets, the strongest effects appear in specific tail combinations. Notably, we identify a divergence in physical climate risk pricing: while low-level risk news supports clean energy valuations, extreme physical risk news disproportionately penalizes high-energy-intensity blockchain assets. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of accounting for nonlinear dynamics and the "green–brown" technology spectrum when evaluating asset resilience.

title: Enhancing the Prudential Framework for Securities Firms

detail.title: Enhancing the Prudential Framework for Securities Firms

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Development Institute (KDI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Despite increasing risk exposure from expanding assets and leverage among large securities firms, the current Net Capital Ratio (NCR) framework does not adequately capture these risks. To strengthen risk sensitivity while maintaining a balance between financial soundness and industry growth, the NCR formula for large securities firms should revert to its pre-2016 structure, and a differentiated regulatory approach tailored to business scope and risk characteristics should apply to small- and medium-sized firms.

title: Why the Capital Region Keeps Growing: Urban Accounting and Spatial Policy Implications

detail.title: Why the Capital Region Keeps Growing: Urban Accounting and Spatial Policy Implications

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Development Institute (KDI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Population concentration in the Seoul Metropolitan Area has continued unabated since the 1970s. In the 2010s, diverging productivity drove this trend—gains in semiconductor and knowledge-based sectors in the capital region versus losses in manufacturing-oriented regional cities. Planned city projects, including Sejong, heavily prioritized infrastructure provision, yielding limited productivity growth and only modest population inflows. To achieve balanced development, spatial policy should move beyond infrastructure investment to boosting regional productivity. Furthermore, narrowing the divide between the capital region and outer regions may necessitate accepting some disparities within outer areas.

title: Economic Development and Democratic Stability in Presidential and Parliamentary Systems: A Cross-National Study, 2000-2023

detail.title: Economic Development and Democratic Stability in Presidential and Parliamentary Systems: A Cross-National Study, 2000-2023
detail.abstract: This paper examines how government system type shapes democratic stability across more than 100 countries from 2000 to 2023. Using country-level cross-sectional data and V-Dem liberal democracy scores, I estimate interaction models to test whether the effect of presidential, parliamentary, and semi-presidential systems depends on economic development. The results show that system type has a conditional relationship with democratic volatility: presidential systems are associated with lower volatility in low-income contexts, while parliamentary systems are associated with greater stability at higher levels of development. The crossover point occurs at approximately $14,000 GDP per capita (PPP). These findings suggest that institutional effects on democracy are context-dependent rather than universal, with important implications for constitutional design in democratizing states.

title: 북한 산업⋅ 기업 데이터베이스를 통한 북한 경제구조 분석 (Revisitng the DPRK Economy: Structural Evidence from Firms and Industries)
affiliations: Korea Development Institute (KDI) - Department of North Korean Economy and Korea Development Institute (KDI)

detail.title: 북한 산업⋅ 기업 데이터베이스를 통한 북한 경제구조 분석 (Revisitng the DPRK Economy: Structural Evidence from Firms and Industries)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Development Institute (KDI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Korean Abstract: 
본 연구는 북한의 산업·기업 DB를 활용하여 북한의 경제구조를 분석하고자 했다. DB를 통하여 북한의 기업 및 산업을 미시적 차원에서 분석하는 한편, 그 결과를 인공위성 지표와 교차 검증하는 과정을 담았다.

제2장에서는 산업연구원의 DB 원자료를 받아 2000년부터 2024년까지 검토하고 재구성하였다. 연도별로 단절된 파일을 하나의 형태로 구축하고 중복되는 값을 삭제했으며, 각각 다르게 나타난 기업명은 통일시켰다. 다음으로 동일한 기업임에도 식별 변수가 불일치하는 경우에는 하나의 기준으로 정리하였으며, 필요할 경우 산업코드, 행정구역 등을 추가했다. 이렇게 본 연구에서 재구성된 DB는 기존 산업연구원의 DB와 비교하여 기업 관찰 수가 3,557개에서 3,973개로, 전체 보도 건수는 86,116건에서 153,047건으로 증가했다.

제3장에서는 북한 기업의 분포와 변화 양상을 분석하여 매체 보도가 단순한 선전용이 아니라 일정한 경제적 함의를 지녔다는 점을 확인했다. 먼저 산업별 보도 비중은 한국은행 산업별 GDP 비율과 높은 상관성을 보였으며, 투자 보도는 1~2년 후 생산 보도의 증가로 이어지는 유의미한 경향을 확인했다. 

제4장에서는 재구성한 북한 산업·기업 DB를 통해 북한 산업에 대한 다각적 분석을 수행하였다. 산업별로는 시기에 따라 산업 보도와 기타 보도의 추세가 다르게 나타났으며, 이는 해당 산업의 생산과 투자 활동이 해당 시점에 얼마나 활발한지 혹은 침체되어 있는지와 밀접한 관련이 있는 것으로 보였다. 
제5장에서는 재구성된 DB와 위성관측 야간조도를 결합해 패널 회귀분석과 이벤트-스터디 분석을 수행함으로써 보도된 ‘투자’·‘생산’이 실제 조업 및 전력 사용 증가와 연계되는지 간접적으로 확인했다. 결과에 따르면, 투자·생산 보도는 모두 야간조도와 유의한 양(+)의 상관관계를 보였다. 이벤트-스터디 분석에서는 투자 기사를 ‘이벤트’로 두고, 사건 시점인 투자 보도 한 달 전을 기준으로 사후 효과를 추정하였다. 그 결과, 사건 이후 0~12개월 동안의 평균효과는 약 7.1%로 5% 수준에서 통계적으로 유의하였으며, 개별 시차 계수도 7~12개월 구간에 유의한 양(+)의 효과가 집중되었다. 

종합하면, 본 연구는 북한 매체의 보도를 단순한 선전물로 치부하지 않고, 경제정책 방향, 산업별 우선순위, 기업활동 실태 등을 간접적으로 파악할 수 있는 ‘근거’로서 주목했다. 그 결과, 보도가 거시경제적 변화를 직접 보여주지는 못하더라도 산업 혹은 기업 차원의 변화를 미시적으로 추적할 수 있는 일종의 ‘도구’로서 기능할 수 있다는 사실을 확인했다. 나아가 이러한 분석이 위성자료 등 대안 지표를 통해 검증된다면 분석의 잠재력은 한층 더 확장될 수 있을 것으로 기대된다.

English Abstract: 
This study aims to analyze the structure of the North Korean economy by utilizing an industry-firm database constructed from North Korean media reports. By examining firms and industries at the micro level and cross-validating findings with satellite-based indicators, the study assesses whether media reports can provide meaningful insights into actual economic activities.

Overall, this study treats North Korean media reports not merely as propaganda but as a source of indirect evidence for understanding economic policy directions, sectoral priorities, and firm-level activities. While media reports do not directly capture macroeconomic fluctuations, the findings suggest that they can function as a useful tool for tracking micro-level industrial and firm dynamics. The analytical potential of this approach may be further enhanced through continued validation using alternative data sources such as satellite imagery.

title: 새로운 재정정책 충격 식별에 따른 경제적 효과: 서술적 분석방법 (Economic Effects of Identified Exogenous Tax Policy Shocks: A Narrative Approach for Korea)

detail.title: 새로운 재정정책 충격 식별에 따른 경제적 효과: 서술적 분석방법 (Economic Effects of Identified Exogenous Tax Policy Shocks: A Narrative Approach for Korea)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Development Institute (KDI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Korean Abstract: 

본 연구는 재정정책 효과 추정치가 연구별로 크게 달라지는 주요 원인 중 하나인 충격 식별의 어려움에 주목하여, 서술적(narrative) 자료에 기반한 방식으로 우리나라의 외생적 조세정책 충격 시계열(2005~23년)을 구축하고, 이를 활용해 조세정책의 단기 거시경제효과를 실증적으로 점검하는 것을 목적으로 한다.

구축된 외생적 조세정책 충격은 기존의 세수 변동 자료에 비해 경기변동과의 연관성이 상대적으로 낮은 모습을 보여, 경기변동분이 혼입되어 있는 재정 변수 대신 정책당국의 재량적 정책 조치에 보다 근접한 충격으로 활용될 가능성을 시사한다. 또한 경기 예측오차(surprise) 기반 점검 등 외생성 검토를 병행하여, 재정수입 변화를 그대로 충격으로 사용할 때 발생할 수 있는 내생성 문제를 해결하고자 하였다.

베이지안 VAR 모형을 이용한 실증분석 결과, 외생적 조세감세 충격은 대체로 실질 GDP와 물가를 유의하게 증가시키는 방향으로 작용하는 것으로 나타났다. 세목별로는 노동세 감세가 상대적으로 큰 GDP 확대 효과를 보이는 반면, 소비세 감세는 GDP 효과가 제한적인 데 비해 세수 감소가 뚜렷한 경향이 관찰되었다. 자본세 감세는 효과 발현에 시차가 존재하면서 단기 세수 감소폭이 상대적으로 크게 나타나는 모습이 확인되어, 세목별 조세정책은 경기대응·세수·정책목표 측면에서 상이한 파급경로를 가질 수 있음을 시사한다. 한편, 감세 이후 총조세수입 반응이 유의하지 않게 나타나는 경우도 있는데, 이는 감세로 인한 세수 감소 효과와 GDP 상승에 따른 세원 확대 효과가 혼재된 결과로 해석할 수 있다.

본 연구는 특정 세목에 대한 단정적 정책 처방을 제시하기보다는, 조세정책 충격을 보다 투명하게 식별하고 정량화하는 자료 구축의 틀을 제시하고자 한다. 또한 세목별·목적별 조세정책이 단기 거시지표와 세수에 미치는 상대적 패턴을 제시함으로써 향후 세제개편과 재정운용 논의의 근거로 활용하고자 한다.

English Abstract: 

This study addresses a key challenge in estimating the macroeconomic effects of fiscal policy: the difficulty of credibly identifying policy shocks. Using a narrative approach, we construct a quarterly series of exogenous tax policy shocks for Korea over 2005~2023 and use it to examine the short-run macroeconomic effects of tax policy.

The identified exogenous tax shocks exhibit a weaker association with business-cycle fluctuations than conventional measures based on observed tax revenue changes, suggesting that they may better capture discretionary policy actions rather than automatic stabilizers. We further assess exogeneity using checks based on GDP forecast errors (“surprises”), aiming to mitigate endogeneity concerns that arise when revenue fluctuations are used directly as shocks.

Empirical analysis based on a Bayesian vector autoregression (BVAR) indicates that exogenous tax cuts generally raise real GDP and prices in the short run. The effects vary across tax categories: labor tax cuts show relatively larger expansionary impacts on output, while consumption tax cuts display limited output effects despite pronounced revenue losses. Capital tax cuts tend to operate with longer lags, accompanied by relatively large short-run revenue declines. These patterns suggest that tax policy can affect the economy through heterogeneous transmission channels depending on the tax base, policy objectives, and the revenueoutput trade-offs. We also find that the response of total tax revenue after tax cuts is sometimes statistically insignificant, consistent with offsetting forces between direct revenue reductions and revenue gains induced by higher output.

Rather than offering prescriptive recommendations for specific taxes, this study provides a transparent framework for identifying and quantifying tax policy shocks and documents the relative patterns of macroeconomic and revenue responses across tax types and motivations. Important limitations remain, including residual uncertainty in narrative classifications when reforms pursue multiple objectives and the need for additional robustness analyses given the sample length and shock frequency. Future research could refine classification rules, compare alternative identification strategies, and integrate spending shocks to strengthen policy implications.

title: Rational Capture Theory in Fraudulent Architectures

detail.title: Rational Capture Theory in Fraudulent Architectures
detail.abstract: A growing body of research tracks the global rise of increasingly refined investment frauds, including those euphemistically-and quite cruelly-termed "pig-butchering." Prevailing explanations tend to focus on isolated tactics: social engineering, appeals to authority, or incremental commitments. But such accounts leave a key question hanging in the air: why do educated, critically-minded individuals continue to participate even after encountering signals that something is amiss? The usual story of gullibility begins to look unconvincing when doubt itself is present, yet engagement persists. This article introduces Rationality Capture Theory to explain how modern investment fraud operates not by silencing rational thought, but by structuring it. Based on a longitudinal qualitative case study of a platform-based equity scheme, the analysis shows how differentiated roles, interface design, and procedural sequencing redirect analytical effort into procedural compliance through a mechanism of analytic containment. The findings demonstrate how multiple manipulation techniques cohere within a unified operating logic that sustains engagement over time, including during post-collapse phases framed as juridical or recovery processes. By shifting attention from individual susceptibility to fraudulent architecture, the study advances consumer research on vulnerability, extends theories of persuasion beyond isolated tactics, and identifies system-level markers relevant for consumer protection and platform governance.

title: Locked In And Locked Out: How Cusma's Digital Trade Architecture Constrains Canadian Sovereignty-And Where The Exits Still Exist

detail.title: Locked In And Locked Out: How Cusma's Digital Trade Architecture Constrains Canadian Sovereignty-And Where The Exits Still Exist
detail.abstract:
CUSMA’s digital trade chapter does not merely open Canadian markets. It closes off Canadian legislative options. Article 19.12 prohibits Canada from requiring foreign cloud providers to store data in Canada. Article 19.16 shields the algorithms that determine credit approvals, hiring decisions, and content moderation from Canadian regulatory audit. Article 19.17 transplants U.S. Section 230 platform immunity into binding Canadian treaty law, regardless of what Canada’s Parliament or the United States Congress chooses to do domestically. These are not trade rules. They are permanent delegations of Canadian legislative authority to foreign preferences.

This Article systematically maps the legal exits that remain within CUSMA’s digital architecture—and explains why Canada has not used them. It identifies five levels of exception available within Chapter 19: scope exclusions for government procurement and government-held information; article-specific conditional exceptions; clarifying clauses that preserve existing policy space; cross-chapter importation of non-conforming measures through Article 19.2(4); and Chapter 32 horizontal exceptions, including the essential security exception whose good faith/plausibility standard—established in Riverside Coffee, LLC v. Republic of Nicaragua—is materially more accessible than the GATS Article XIV necessity test. It further addresses the standards-sovereignty constraint in Chapter 11, the intellectual property lock-in in Chapter 20, the geopolitical veto in Article 32.10, and the double lock-in created by parallel CUSMA and CPTPP obligations.

The 2026 CUSMA Review is the only scheduled opportunity within the existing agreement cycle for Canada to reclaim the regulatory space it surrendered in 2018—often without fully understanding what it was giving away. The exits this Article maps are only useful if Canada arrives at the review table with domestic legislation in force, institutional capacity built, and the political will to walk through them. The animating strategic principle of this analysis is what this author has called “Code Before Clause”: Canada must establish the domestic digital regulatory code—legislation, standards, institutional capacity, and political will—before it arrives at the review table to negotiate trade agreement clauses.

detail.abstract: Nepal's National Identity Card (NID) programme enrolled over 17.2 million citizens by mid-2025, yet only 2.3 million had collected their cards and the NID remained connected to fewer than ten services nationally. This paper asks: under what architectural conditions can a foundational identity system achieve cross-domain interoperability without creating exclusion or surveillance risk? Drawing on infrastructure theory, data justice, and digital era governance frameworks, it analyses six national digital identity systems to derive two design propositions: federated architectures correlate with lower breach severity, and citizen audit visibility correlates with voluntary adoption. From these propositions and Nepal's constitutional constraints-including the Supreme Court's 2024 jurisprudence on citizenship certificate primacy-the paper proposes the Nepal Civic Identity Stack: a six-layer federated architecture built on open standards (OpenID Connect, MOSIP, X-Road) with a citizen-centric consent layer. Eight integration domains are prioritised through a scoring matrix; legal analysis identifies critical gaps in Nepal's Privacy Act 2075 using GDP-normalised penalty comparisons and Nissenbaum's contextual integrity framework. The paper advances the Federated Legibility Principle as a transferable framework for fragile-federation contexts. Limitations, including the absence of primary fieldwork, are acknowledged explicitly.

title: A Coordinated Framework for Artificial Intelligence: Governance Architecture for Risk-Proportionate Oversight Under Symmetric Risk Obligation

detail.title: A Coordinated Framework for Artificial Intelligence: Governance Architecture for Risk-Proportionate Oversight Under Symmetric Risk Obligation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: The companion paper, Beyond Precaution, argues that risk assessment, not precautionary principle, under Symmetric Risk Obligation (SRO) is the appropriate governing principle for artificial intelligence. This paper operationalizes that argument. It specifies the institutional architecture, jurisdictional assignments, evaluation processes, and political mechanisms required to implement SRO-compliant AI governance using existing federal statutory authority. Drawing on the 1986 Coordinated Framework for the Regulation of Biotechnology as a structural precedent, and on direct experience securing the first FDA and USDA market authorizations for cultivated meat, this paper proposes a Coordinated Framework for Artificial Intelligence: a three-tier governance architecture with agency-specific jurisdictional assignments, a detailed pre-deployment evaluation process for frontier AI systems, and a compromise architecture designed to bring stakeholders with fundamentally different interests to a common table. No new agency is required. No new legislation is proposed and no new statutory authority claimed. This paper provides the blueprint for the coordinating document.

detail.abstract: The international legal order, established upon the ruins of the Second World War with the explicit goal of preventing the "scourge of war," is currently facing a systemic collapse. This dissolution is not merely the result of shifting power dynamics but is driven by a deliberate and sustained campaign of unilateralism by the United States, which has increasingly prioritized national interests over the collective norms of the United Nations Charter. The military intervention in Venezuela on January 3, 2026, serves as the quintessential manifestation of this trend, representing a departure from even the pretense of multilateral legitimacy toward a doctrine of explicit regional domination and resource securitization. By analyzing the long arc of American interventionism, the legal mechanisms used to bypass sovereign immunity, and the growing resistance from the Global South, it becomes evident that the role of the United States as a "world police" has transitioned into a primary driver of global instability and a violator of the very principles of self-determination it once claimed to uphold.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence approaches operational supremacy, traditional governance faces an existential "alignment problem." This paper proposes a radical architectural framework: the Reconfigurable Cage. By applying a Functional Decoupling of Sovereignty, we separate the Technical Layer (AI-driven execution) from the Deliberative Layer (human value definition). Central to this model is Update Authority, the exclusive, non-delegable human right to revise the algorithmic "bars" of the cage. To ensure the integrity of this authority, the model introduces Autonomous Algorithmic Appointment (AAA) for meritocratic screening, Economic Saturation to insulate human deliberators from material corruption, and Distributed Algorithmic Oversight (DAOv). The Reconfigurable Cage does not eliminate the right to be wrong; it institutionalizes the conditions under which human error remains sovereign rather than catastrophic. Ultimately, the purpose of the Cage is not to perfect humanity, but to protect the fragile dignity of imperfect agents.

title: Social Value Currency (SVC) with Universal Dividend

detail.title: Social Value Currency (SVC) with Universal Dividend
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Social Value Currency (SVC), a sovereign monetary framework designed to replace debt-based money creation with issuance directly linked to the net creation of real economic value. Under SVC, the monetary base is adjusted annually in accordance with estimated changes in socially produced real net value, excluding purely speculative asset revaluations. Positive net value creation generates an equal per-capita universal dividend credited to all citizens, allowing aggregate demand to track productive growth without structural reliance on credit expansion. In periods of contraction, symmetric adjustments are applied exclusively to monetary balances, preserving physical assets and maintaining accounting consistency. A key institutional feature is the strict separation between the sovereign unit of account and private financial contracts: no credit instrument may create SVC units, thereby preventing endogenous debt-driven monetary expansion while permitting voluntary investment through equity participation and private lending outside the monetary base. SVC aims to eliminate interest-bearing money as a structural source of financial rent, stabilize the relationship between money and real value, and embed an automatic distributive mechanism within the monetary architecture. The paper situates SVC within the broader literature on sovereign money, social dividends, and value-based monetary reform

detail.title: Reusable Rocket Design for Low-Altitude Smog Monitoring Using Eco-Friendly Fuel
detail.abstract: The escalating crisis of smog in urban centers like that of Lahore emphasizes the necessity of a rapid, localized atmospheric intervention technologies. This study presents the aerodynamic design and ballistic simulation of a low-cost and reusable rocket developed for fast and efficient Hygroscopic Aerosol Dispersion (HAD) through cheaper means then the conventional methods. Unlike conventional cloud-seeding aircraft, which are logistically constrained, this groundlaunched system utilizes a solid-propellant (KNSU) motor to deliver a 1.5 kg payload to a target altitude of 2.19 km much more easily and efficiently. The vehicle design was optimized using OpenRocket software, achieving a high static stability margin of calibers 6.1 to ensure flight safety under turbulent conditions. Computational modeling of the trajectory confirms a vertical apogee velocity of 0 m/s, triggering an automated parachute recovery system for safe descent. The proposed design offers a scalable, indigenous engineering solution for targeted precipitation enhancement and particulate matter reduction.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Verified Property Record (VPR), a canonical and machine-interrogable representation model for real-world real estate assets in the context of the emerging Cognitive Web. As artificial intelligence systems increasingly act as primary intermediaries in search, evaluation, and decision-making processes, traditional narrative-based property representations become structurally inadequate.

The VPR proposes an entity-centric framework that separates representation from presentation, enabling versioning, citability, provenance tracking, and deterministic evaluation. Rather than functioning as a commercial platform or marketplace, the VPR articulates a conceptual and epistemic model for how real-world assets may be represented for automated reasoning systems.

The paper positions real estate as a reference domain demonstrating the feasibility of canonical representation for complex physical assets. It argues that structured, persistent, and interrogable records are foundational for machine-readable trust in the Cognitive Web.

title: A Conditional Political Typology Framework for Understanding Political Actor Dynamics Under Varying Economic and Institutional Conditions

detail.title: A Conditional Political Typology Framework for Understanding Political Actor Dynamics Under Varying Economic and Institutional Conditions
detail.abstract: This paper presents the Irawadi Dynamic Model, a conditional political typology framework that maps the relationships between four distinct political actor profiles and the structural conditions-primarily economic performance and institutional trust-that determine which profiles gain or lose political power at any given moment. Unlike conventional left-right political analysis, the model makes no normative judgments about which actors are morally correct. Instead, it treats political outcomes as conditional emergent properties of the interaction between actor characteristics and environmental variables. The model identifies four archetypal political profiles: the Apolitical Discontented (A1), the Progressive Left-Liberal (A2), the National Conservative (A3), and the Authoritarian Paternalist (A4). It demonstrates that these profiles interact differently under three distinct economic and institutional conditions-stability, deterioration, and collapse-and that the directionality of these transitions carries significant asymmetric ratchet effects. The model is validated against historical cases including Weimar Germany, post-Soviet Eastern Europe, and contemporary global electoral trends. Implications for democratic resilience and the conditions under which authoritarian consolidation sequences become probable are discussed. The model's primary contribution is its integration of psychological typology, group interaction dynamics, economic Permana Putra Irawadi The Irawadi Dynamic Model conditioning, and historical pattern recognition into a single parsimonious framework, offering explanatory power that exceeds the conventional left-right binary while remaining accessible to non-specialist audiences.

title: Evidence from Examiner Assignment

detail.title: Evidence from Examiner Assignment
detail.abstract: Majority-female inventor teams at the USPTO exhibit a raw grant-rate gap of 5.6 percentage points, nearly all of which reflects technology sorting: the gap falls to 0.14 percentage points within art unit and filing year. Using administrative assignment of 5.9 million applications to examiners within art unit and year cells, I show that female examiners are stricter overall (1.45 percentage points lower grant rate) yet grant a higher share of patents to female inventor teams (0.55 percentage points). This composition effect is concentrated in art units with greater female inventor prevalence and grows with examiner experience.

title: Algorithmic Constitutionalism and the "Update Authority" Human Sovereignty and the Right to Noble Failure in the Age of AI Governance

detail.title: Algorithmic Constitutionalism and the "Update Authority" Human Sovereignty and the Right to Noble Failure in the Age of AI Governance
