detail.abstract:
Fiduciary duty remains a foundational principle in institutional governance, yet its evaluation has become increasingly challenging as organizations grow more complex, delegated, and model-informed. Traditional assessments that rely heavily on outcomes or ex post performance provide weak signals of fiduciary quality in environments characterized by uncertainty and fragmented accountability.

This paper reframes fiduciary duty as a decision-making discipline under uncertainty and argues that fiduciary failure is most often a governance design problem rather than a single bad decision.

It introduces a Process-Based Fiduciary Assessment (PBFA) framework that enables fiduciary boards and oversight bodies to evaluate decision integrity through governance structure, uncertainty management, incentive alignment, monitoring, and escalation capacity.

By shifting oversight focus from outcomes to process quality, the framework supports proportional oversight, preserves legitimate risk-taking, and strengthens institutional accountability across asset classes and organizational forms.

title: Looking for Risk: Volatility Bounds in Macro

detail.title: Looking for Risk: Volatility Bounds in Macro
detail.abstract: We characterize the gap between the equity risk premium (ERP) and its SVIX-implied lower bound as an equilibrium object, increasing in the correlation of valuations and returns, their relative volatility, and risk aversion. Higher risk premia need not be reflected in options-implied volatility. Yet, models resolving the equity premium puzzle through high risk aversion will tend to understate the lower bound and risk-neutral variance of returns. Applying our findings to a RBC economy with disasters, we consider an increase in their probability leading to a 1 p.p. rise in the ERP, but a negligible rise in the SVIX-implied bound (10 b.p.).

title: The Economic Impact of Establishing Offshore Wind Energy Capacity: Evidence from Ireland

detail.title: The Economic Impact of Establishing Offshore Wind Energy Capacity: Evidence from Ireland

detail.abstract: Many countries are expanding their production of renewable energy to decrease dependence on fossil fuels and combat climate change. Offshore wind represents one such source of renewable energy. Ireland has committed to raising its offshore wind capacity to 5GW by the year 2030, with further capacity increases envisaged. This paper uses input-output analysis to assess the economic impact of an expanded offshore wind sector in Ireland. We use the Arklow Bank Wind Park 2, a proposed 800MW offshore wind project off the coast of Co. Wicklow, as a case study. For the capital expenditure (CAPEX) stage of the project, the model shows small output multipliers of 1.05 and 1.07 for the Type I and Type II multipliers respectively. This is due to the large reliance on imports in this phase of the project. Larger multipliers of 1.29 (Type I) and 1.49 (Type II) are seen during the operational phase of the project. The model predicts yearly gross value added of €14.82 million associated with the development. It is estimated that 444 annualised full time equivalent (aFTE) jobs will be generated in the CAPEX phase while 43 aFTE positions will be created during the operational stage. We find that while there is there is high direct investment associated with proposed offshore wind projects in Ireland, the low level of local contribution, especially in the CAPEX phase, means that the projects’ knock-on economic impact for the Irish economy will be limited.

detail.abstract: Institutional investment outcomes are typically explained through asset allocation, strategy selection, and market conditions. Yet across public markets, private markets, and real assets, institutions pursuing similar strategies under comparable conditions routinely experience sharply divergent results. This paper argues that governance quality-not asset class exposure-is the more consistent determinant of institutional investment outcomes. Governance is examined not as compliance, disclosure, or ESG integration, but as institutional infrastructure-the system through which authority is allocated, incentives are structured, decisions are reviewed, and accountability is enforced over time. Drawing on cross-asset institutional experience, the paper introduces a four-pillar governance framework-authority allocation, incentive architecture, information traceability, and accountability with adaptationand applies it across asset classes including public markets, private equity, private credit, real assets, direct investing, quantitative strategies, and emerging digital structures. The analysis shows that while governance failures differ in form across asset classes, they converge structurally. By reframing governance quality as primary institutional infrastructure and a fiduciary multiplier, the paper provides a system-level lens for understanding why similar investments produce divergent outcomes and how institutions can improve durability under complexity without prescribing specific organizational structures.

detail.abstract: In this study we examine the potential effects of the 2026 Gulf conflict on global oil markets, with particular focus on disruptions to maritime transport through the Strait of Hormuz. To assess the implications for oil markets, this study employs a GARCH-MIDAS framework that decomposes oil price volatility into short-run financial dynamics and long-run macrofinancial drivers, including geopolitical risk, financial uncertainty, and shipping disruptions. The estimation results reveal strong volatility persistence and heavy-tailed shocks in oil returns. Among the long-run drivers, disruptions to maritime transport emerge as the most economically significant factor influencing oil market volatility. The estimated model is combined with scenario simulations of potential Strait of Hormuz closures lasting one, three, and six months. The results indicate that maritime disruptions generate significant short-term oil price spikes as markets incorporate precautionary geopolitical risk premia. Under a one-month disruption, the median oil price rises to about $110 per barrel before gradually declining toward $75 as shipping conditions stabilize. A three-month disruption produces a larger peak price of roughly $131 per barrel, followed by gradual adjustment as tanker rerouting and inventory drawdowns mitigate supply constraints. In contrast, a six-month disruption leads to more persistent price pressures, with median prices peaking near $142 per barrel and remaining slightly elevated at about $93 per barrel by the end of the period due to tightening global oil balances and sustained logistical constraints. Overall, the findings highlight the critical role of maritime disruptions in transmitting geopolitical shocks to global oil markets.

title: Social Media Platforms as Democratizing Infrastructure
affiliations: and The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Social Media Platforms as Democratizing Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Social media platforms are theorized to either equalize access to economic opportunity by circumventing traditional gatekeepers or reproduce existing structural inequalities through algorithmic bias. Despite extensive theoretical debate, causal evidence examining these positions remains scarce. This study leverages Universal Music Group’s removal of its music catalog from TikTok in February 2024 as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate the causal effect of social media platform visibility on artists’ economic outcomes and to examine whether that effect is distributed equally across structurally heterogeneous artists. Analyzing 21,150 artist-day observations using a Difference-in-Differences framework, we find that UMG-affiliated artists experienced a significant decline in Spotify streaming performance following their removal from TikTok, confirming that social media platform visibility constitutes meaningful economic infrastructure. Critically, this effect was not uniform: artists from historically underrepresented backgrounds, particularly non-male artists, suffered disproportionately greater losses, supporting the equalizer hypothesis and providing causal evidence that TikTok functions as democratizing economic infrastructure for underrepresented artists. Drawing on intersectionality theory and distributive justice principles, we argue that corporate intermediaries making platform-level decisions on behalf of structurally heterogeneous artist groups bear a substantive ethical obligation to assess the distributional consequences of those decisions, not merely their average impact. These findings contribute to the business ethics, social media platform, and social equity literatures, and carry implications for record labels, platform governance, and digital content policy.

detail.abstract: Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) are the last line of healthcare defense for 60 million rural Americans across 1,377 designated facilities. Despite federal cost-based reimbursement protections, the sector operates at a median operating margin of approximately-2.3%, with denial rates near 8.7%, labor cost ratios exceeding 58%, and 146-196 closures recorded since 2005. Proposed federal budget reductions under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) threaten up to 300 additional closures. This paper introduces GRHD: Get Rural Health Donea benchmark-driven computational framework that defines, measures, and closes the CAH performance gap through five structured pillars: Revenue Intelligence, Clinical Quality Engineering, Operational Architecture, Workforce Stabilization, and Infrastructure & Connectivity. Central to GRHD is the CAHSP score (Critical Assessment of Hospital Sustainability & Performance), a weighted composite index ([0, 100]) modeled directly on the CASP benchmark that enabled AlphaFold 2's breakthrough in protein structure prediction. CAHSP establishes a "dual mandate joint floor": solutions must achieve a Financial Index ≥ 0.75 and a Clinical Quality Index ≥ 0.70 simultaneously, with no quality-for-margin tradeoff permitted. We formalize the optimization problem using Lagrangian methods under 42 CFR §485 regulatory constraints, a gap function G(t) = S *-S(t) governing dual-mandate trajectory, and a Bertsimas-Sim robust reformulation tolerating HCRIS parameter variance. Target performance across the Minimum Viable CAH Infrastructure (MV-CAHI)-25 beds, 1-2 IT FTE, rural broadband at 25/3 Mbps-is CAHSP ≥ 85, representing the equivalent of AlphaFold's GDT_TS ≥ 90 for the CAH problem. A phased WA/MT pilot roadmap and national scaling pathway to all 1,355+ CAHs are presented.

title: How Japanese Consumer Behaviour Differs From Western Markets

detail.title: How Japanese Consumer Behaviour Differs From Western Markets
detail.abstract: The cultural environment is a critical component in identifying how consumers entertain their behavior towards brands; therefore, how they purchase and perceive themselves against the attributes of a product will play a large role in successful international operations for companies that deal with a broad range of demographics and cultures. In this paper, I will compare the consumer behavior in Japan to that of Western markets (the United States and Europe). Group consensus, harmony and being detail oriented are values many Japanese consumers will place higher importance on than the values placed by many Western consumers (individuality, personal expression, and convenience). Therefore, this cultural foundation will not only dictate the types of products purchased by these consumers, but how they interact with the brands when making purchasing decisions.
